en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek leaves the verb unstated.

01.r: The Pharisees and scribes, set against what has just been said.
01.n: The pronoun is written out, which the verb does not need. Abbott-Smith notes that the nominative is used for emphasis or contrast.

03.n: A present tense: what they habitually say.

04.r: Sets up the case they allow.
04.n: Abbott-Smith: a conditional particle for something 'under certain circumstances actual or liable to happen'.

05.n: An aorist subjunctive after 'if': a case that may arise.

06.r: Anyone, a son speaking to his parents.

07.r: The article, which English renders 'his'; 'to' comes from the dative case of the noun.

12.r: A word declaring something dedicated to God, and so withheld from ordinary use.
12.n: Abbott-Smith: from Hebrew קָרְבָּן, 'an offering, a gift offered to God', citing only this verse. Mark keeps the Hebrew word and then explains it.

13.r: Introduces Mark's explanation of the foreign word.

15.r: Mark's Greek for Corban: a gift offered to God.
15.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses this word chiefly for קָרְבָּן, the very Hebrew word Mark explains, and lists this verse among gifts and sacrifices to God. The ASV's 'Given to God' and the BSB's 'a gift devoted to God' make that sense explicit.

16.r: Any help the parents might have had from their son.

17.r: With the word before, makes it general: 'whatever'.
17.n: The same word as 'if' earlier in the verse; after a relative it widens it to 'whatever'.

18.r: The source of the help: the son.

20.r: The support the parents could have had from him.
20.n: An aorist passive subjunctive. Abbott-Smith derives the verb from ὄφελος and gives 'to help, benefit, do good, profit'. The KJV's 'he shall be free' at the end of the verse answers to nothing in this verse's Greek; the sentence runs on into the next verse.
